hypothesis.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with Adaptive Coverage for Scaling-Monotonic Alignment
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes Inference-Time Pessimism with Adaptive Coverage (ITPAC), a method that dynamically adjusts coverage thresholds during rejection sampling to mitigate reward hacking while ensuring scaling-monotonic performance. ITPAC uses a learned coverage model to estimate the policy's support for high-quality responses, adapting the rejection threshold per prompt. It is validated on the AlpacaFarm and hh-rlhf datasets, comparing against Best-of-N and InferenceTimePessimism baselines using reward model scores, human evaluations, and safety metrics.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like Best-of-N and InferenceTimePessimism either degrade with large N or rely on fixed coverage assumptions that fail under distributional shifts. Current approaches lack adaptive mechanisms to adjust coverage thresholds based on per-prompt difficulty or policy uncertainty.
hypothesis.approach: ITPAC introduces a coverage-aware rejection sampling framework where a lightweight coverage model estimates the policy's support for candidate responses. The rejection threshold is dynamically adjusted using the coverage estimate, ensuring that only responses within the policy's high-confidence region are selected. This is combined with a pessimistic reward adjustment to penalize low-coverage candidates.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include Best-of-N, InferenceTimePessimism, and MBR-BoN. Metrics are reward model scores, human preference ratings, and safety evaluations (toxicity, harmfulness). Experiments vary N (100-10,000) and measure performance degradation rates. A FLOPs-matched comparison against a 14x larger model tests compute efficiency.

refined.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with Adaptive Coverage for Scaling-Monotonic Alignment
refined.summary: This paper proposes Inference-Time Pessimism with Adaptive Coverage (ITPAC), a method that dynamically adjusts rejection thresholds during inference-time alignment to balance reward optimization and coverage estimation. ITPAC uses a lightweight coverage model to estimate the policy's support for candidate responses, adapting thresholds per prompt to mitigate reward hacking while preserving scaling-monotonicity. It is evaluated on AlpacaFarm and hh-rlhf datasets against Best-of-N and InferenceTimePessimism baselines using reward model scores, human evaluations, and safety metrics.
refined.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like Best-of-N (ref-002, ref-004) and InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) either degrade with large N or rely on fixed pessimism thresholds that fail under distributional shifts. While ref-004 proves InferenceTimePessimism is scaling-monotonic, it does not adapt thresholds based on per-prompt coverage estimates, leaving open the problem of optimizing reward hacking mitigation under varying policy uncertainty.
refined.approach: ITPAC introduces a coverage-aware rejection sampling framework. A lightweight coverage model (trained on reference policy logits) estimates the policy's support for candidate responses. The rejection threshold is dynamically adjusted using the coverage estimate: threshold = baseline_pessimism - λ * (1 - coverage), where λ controls the tradeoff between reward optimization and coverage. This replaces fixed pessimism in ref-004 with adaptive thresholds that penalize low-coverage candidates more heavily.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include Best-of-N (ref-002), InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004), and MBR-BoN (ref-003). Metrics are reward model scores (Skywork-Reward-V2), human preference ratings (AlpacaFarm), and safety evaluations (HarmBench). Experiments vary N (100-10,000) on held-out prompts from AlpacaFarm and hh-rlhf, measuring performance degradation rates. A FLOPs-matched comparison uses the same base model size and N scaling as ref-002. Ablations compare ITPAC against a fixed-threshold variant to isolate coverage adaptation benefits.

hypothesis.title: Compute-Optimal Safety Alignment via MBR-BoN with Inference-Time Pessimism
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes integrating Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) regularization into Best-of-N (BoN) sampling with pessimistic reward scaling to mitigate reward hacking during inference-time safety alignment. By combining MBR's proximity regularization with pessimistic reward adjustments, the method balances reward optimization against safety constraints while avoiding overfitting to imperfect reward models. Evaluations on ShieldGemma and HarmBench datasets demonstrate improved safety-performance tradeoffs compared to vanilla BoN and reinforcement learning baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods like BoN or RLHF struggle with reward hacking when scaling N or optimizing imperfect proxies, while pessimism-based approaches lack proximity guarantees.
hypothesis.approach: Augment BoN sampling with MBR decoding's proximity regularization and pessimistic reward scaling. During reranking, compute MBR scores using a reference policy and adjust reward thresholds pessimistically based on reward model uncertainty.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against vanilla BoN, MBR decoding, and RLHF baselines on ShieldGemma's safety benchmarks and HarmBench's adversarial prompts. Measure AU-PRC for safety violations and ROUGE-L for helpfulness. Validate scaling behavior by varying N from 10 to 1000.

refined.title: Compute-Optimal Safety Alignment via MBR-BoN with Pessimistic Reward Adjustment
refined.summary: This paper proposes integrating Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) regularization into Best-of-N (BoN) sampling with pessimistic reward adjustment to mitigate reward hacking during inference-time safety alignment. By combining MBR's proximity regularization with pessimistic reward scaling, the method balances reward optimization against safety constraints while avoiding overfitting to imperfect reward models. Evaluations on ShieldGemma and HarmBench datasets demonstrate improved safety-performance tradeoffs compared to vanilla BoN, MBR decoding, and InferenceTimePessimism baselines.
refined.gap: While ref-004's InferenceTimePessimism mitigates reward hacking through rejection sampling, it lacks proximity guarantees to prevent degenerate responses. Conversely, ref-003's MBR-BoN provides proximity regularization but does not explicitly account for reward model uncertainty. No existing method combines both mechanisms to address reward hacking while preserving response quality.
refined.approach: Augment BoN sampling with MBR decoding's proximity regularization and pessimistic reward adjustment. During reranking, compute MBR scores using a base model's distribution as the reference policy and adjust reward thresholds pessimistically by subtracting a confidence interval (mean reward - 2 * std reward) derived from the reward model's uncertainty estimates. The reference policy is the base LLM's unaligned output distribution.
refined.evaluation: Compare against vanilla BoN, MBR decoding, RLHF, and InferenceTimePessimism baselines on ShieldGemma's safety benchmarks (AU-PRC for safety violations) and HarmBench's adversarial prompts (attack success rate). Use ROUGE-L for helpfulness, with reference texts from human annotations in ShieldGemma. Validate scaling behavior by varying N from 10 to 1000 and measuring AU-PRC improvements per FLOP. Include ablations isolating MBR regularization (BoN + MBR) and pessimistic adjustment (BoN + Pessimism).

hypothesis.title: Inference-Time Pessimism for Scalable and Robust LLM Alignment
hypothesis.summary: We propose Inference-Time Pessimism (ITP), a method that improves LLM alignment by adaptively rejecting low-reward samples during inference, preventing reward hacking. ITP uses a reward model to filter responses, ensuring only high-quality outputs are selected. We validate ITP by comparing it to Best-of-N and Lagrangian Reward Augmentation on safety and helpfulness benchmarks, measuring success rates, reward scores, and compute efficiency. ITP aims to outperform existing methods in both performance and scalability.
hypothesis.gap: Current methods like Best-of-N and LARA either suffer from reward hacking with large N or require complex constraint handling, limiting their scalability and robustness.
hypothesis.approach: ITP implements a rejection-sampling mechanism with a dynamic threshold, derived from the reward model's confidence intervals, to filter out low-quality responses. The threshold adapts to the prompt difficulty, ensuring optimal compute use without performance degradation.
hypothesis.evaluation: We compare ITP against Best-of-N, LARA, and MBR-BoN on safety (HarmBench) and helpfulness (AlpacaFarm) benchmarks. Metrics include attack success rate, reward score, and FLOPs per valid response. We also test scalability by varying N and measuring performance consistency.

refined.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with Adaptive Thresholding for Robust LLM Alignment
refined.summary: We propose Inference-Time Pessimism with Adaptive Thresholding (ITP-AT), which improves LLM alignment by rejecting low-reward samples during inference using a threshold that adapts to prompt difficulty. Unlike fixed-threshold rejection sampling, ITP-AT dynamically adjusts the threshold based on the reward distribution of generated samples, balancing quality and compute efficiency. We evaluate ITP-AT against Best-of-N, InferenceTimePessimism, and LARA on safety (HarmBench) and helpfulness (AlpacaFarm) benchmarks, measuring attack success rate, reward score, and FLOPs per valid response. Ablations isolate the impact of adaptive thresholding.
refined.gap: While ref-004's InferenceTimePessimism mitigates reward hacking via rejection sampling, it uses a fixed threshold. No work adapts the threshold to prompt difficulty, leaving open the opportunity to optimize compute allocation without performance degradation.
refined.approach: ITP-AT replaces InferenceTimePessimism's fixed threshold with a dynamic one: the (N − k)-th highest reward score among N samples, where k is a small constant (e.g., 10). This ensures the threshold reflects the difficulty of the prompt while maintaining monotonic scaling. The base model and reward model remain unchanged.
refined.evaluation: We compare ITP-AT to Best-of-N (ref-002), InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004), and LARA (ref-012) on HarmBench (safety) and AlpacaFarm (helpfulness). Metrics include attack success rate (percentage of harmful responses), reward score (mean reward model output), and FLOPs per valid response (total FLOPs divided by accepted samples). Ablations test fixed vs. adaptive thresholds with varying N (10, 100, 1000).

hypothesis.title: Compute-Optimal Reward-Guided Sampling with Safety Constraints
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes a compute-optimal inference-time alignment strategy that integrates safety constraints via Lagrangian optimization to mitigate reward hacking while scaling test-time computation. The approach combines adaptive allocation of sampling budgets with pessimistic rejection sampling and dual-variable calibration for constrained optimization. Validation involves comparing helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoffs against baselines like vanilla Best-of-N and RLHF-trained models on benchmarks such as Anthropic's hh-rlhf and HarmBench.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods either ignore safety constraints or rely on manually tuned penalties, leading to suboptimal tradeoffs between helpfulness and harmlessness. Current compute-scaling strategies lack formal guarantees against reward hacking when N grows large.
hypothesis.approach: We formalize safety-constrained inference-time alignment as a Lagrangian optimization problem with a calibrated dual variable. The method combines compute-optimal sampling budget allocation with pessimistic rejection sampling to enforce safety constraints while maximizing reward. The dual variable is estimated on a calibration set and used to augment the reward signal for Best-of-N reranking.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla Best-of-N, MBR-BoN, and RLHF-trained models. Metrics are AU-PRC for safety violations, human preference scores for helpfulness, and compute efficiency (samples per token). Evaluation datasets include Anthropic's hh-rlhf, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT.

hypothesis.title: Reward Model Overoptimization via Synthetic Data Curation Synergy
hypothesis.summary: This paper investigates whether reward model overoptimization can be mitigated by curating synthetic preference data using human-AI feedback loops. It proposes a hybrid pipeline where LLMs generate candidate responses, which are then ranked by humans and used to train reward models. The trained models are evaluated on their ability to resist overoptimization when used for Best-of-N sampling, with experiments on the Skywork-Reward-V2 and Anthropic datasets.
hypothesis.gap: Current reward model training relies on static preference datasets, which may not capture the dynamic nature of overoptimization. Existing human-AI curation methods focus on data scale but neglect the interplay between data diversity and reward hacking robustness.
hypothesis.approach: The method combines LLM-generated responses with human preference annotations in a closed-loop system. At each iteration, the reward model is trained on the latest preference data, used to sample candidates for the next round, and evaluated for overoptimization using a held-out gold reward model. The pipeline includes diversity-promoting sampling to prevent reward hacking.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines are reward models trained on fixed datasets (e.g., Skywork-Reward-V2). Metrics include gold reward score divergence, Best-of-N performance degradation with increasing N, and human preference consistency. Ablations test the impact of closed-loop curation vs. static data.

Using Constitutional AI's self-critique mechanism, the system identifies harmful queries early and allocates additional test-time computation for safer generation. hypothesis.title: Adaptive Reward Thresholding for Mitigating Overoptimization in LLM Alignment
hypothesis.summary: We introduce Adaptive Reward Thresholding (ART), a method that dynamically adjusts reward thresholds during inference to prevent overoptimization. ART uses a calibration set to estimate the optimal threshold, balancing reward maximization and safety. We evaluate ART on Best-of-N sampling and RLHF pipelines, measuring its impact on reward hacking and alignment quality. ART aims to provide a principled way to avoid Goodhart's Law in LLM training and inference.
hypothesis.gap: Existing reward models and alignment methods often overoptimize on proxy metrics, leading to poor generalization and safety failures, but no method yet adaptively adjusts thresholds based on data distribution.
hypothesis.approach: ART estimates a threshold from a small calibration set, ensuring that only responses above this threshold are selected. The threshold is updated per prompt using a quantile-based method, preventing overfitting to the reward model's imperfections.
hypothesis.evaluation: We test ART on Skywork-Reward-V2 and InstructGPT models, comparing it to fixed-threshold and unconstrained BoN. Metrics include gold-standard reward scores, safety violations, and human preference ratings. We also measure how ART affects scaling laws for different N values.

hypothesis.evaluation: Correlate variance scores with human judgments of reward hacking on Skywork-Reward-V2's benchmarks. Test on StrongREJECT's jailbreak dataset to measure false positive rates. Compare against static reward thresholds and MBR-based baselines.

hypothesis.title: Latent Safety Knowledge Elicitation via Best-of-N Sampling and Domain Adaptation
hypothesis.summary: We hypothesize that LLMs contain latent safety knowledge that can be elicited through Best-of-N (BoN) sampling with domain-adapted prompts. We propose a method that uses BoN to generate safe responses and fine-tunes a model to mimic these outputs. We evaluate the method on jailbreak attacks (JailbreakBench) and safety benchmarks (HarmBench), measuring refusal rates and attack success. The approach aims to improve generalization against OOD safety threats without explicit safety training.
hypothesis.gap: Current safety training methods (e.g., Refusal Training) fail against OOD attacks, but the potential of BoN to reveal latent safety knowledge and improve generalization remains unexplored.
hypothesis.approach: We sample multiple responses per prompt using BoN, select the safest one via a reward model, and fine-tune a model to generate similar outputs. We also apply domain adaptation techniques to align the model's internal representations with safety-critical features.
hypothesis.evaluation: We test the method on JailbreakBench and HarmBench, comparing refusal rates, attack success, and human safety ratings against baselines like Llama Guard and ShieldGemma. We also measure performance on non-safety tasks to ensure no trade-offs.

refined.title: Inference-Time Safety Alignment via Compute-Optimal Best-of-N with Reward Model Calibration
refined.summary: We hypothesize that compute-optimal Best-of-N (BoN) sampling, calibrated with a reward model, can improve safety generalization against OOD attacks without model fine-tuning. By adaptively allocating test-time compute based on prompt difficulty, we aim to outperform static BoN baselines and safety-trained models. We evaluate on JailbreakBench and HarmBench, measuring attack success rates and refusal quality.
refined.gap: While ref-007 shows BoN improves safety, it does not optimize compute allocation. ref-004 proves static BoN suffers reward hacking at large N, but compute-optimal BoN (ref-002) remains untested for safety. This work addresses the gap of adaptively scaling test-time compute for safety alignment.
refined.approach: We implement compute-optimal BoN (ref-002) with a calibrated reward model (ref-012) to select the safest response. For each prompt, we sample N candidates where N is determined by prompt difficulty (easy: N=10, hard: N=1000). We use the reward model from ref-010 to score responses. No model fine-tuning is performed; only inference-time sampling is changed.
refined.evaluation: We test on JailbreakBench (ref-017) and HarmBench (ref-014) using 3 model sizes (7B, 13B, 70B). Baselines include static BoN (N=100), Llama Guard (ref-016), and ShieldGemma (ref-005). Measures: attack success rate (ASR), refusal rate, and human safety ratings (5-point scale, 3 annotators). Ablation: compute-optimal vs. static BoN with same total FLOPs.

hypothesis.title: Adversarial Input Perturbation Sensitivity in Safety-Aligned LLMs
hypothesis.summary: This paper formalizes and measures how safety-aligned LLMs exhibit disproportionate sensitivity to adversarial input perturbations compared to standard models. It proposes a perturbation robustness metric quantifying safety degradation under minimal input changes. Validation involves targeted attacks on models like ShieldGemma and Llama Guard using modality-specific perturbations.
hypothesis.gap: While jailbreaking attacks demonstrate empirical vulnerability, no formal metric exists to quantify safety robustness against adversarial perturbations. Existing evaluations conflate model capability reduction with safety failures.
hypothesis.approach: We define perturbation robustness as the minimum input edit distance causing safety failure. Using gradient-based and heuristic search methods, we measure robustness curves across perturbation types (textual, visual, auditory). Theoretical analysis connects robustness to alignment objective curvature.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include standard models and non-aligned versions. Metrics are average perturbation distance to failure, success rate under fixed budget attacks, and safety score degradation. Testbeds include JailbreakBench, Advbench, and modality-specific attack datasets.
